# Receipts

Public memory should last longer than the news cycle.

## Purpose

Receipts compares a dated public claim with later conduct when the gap has a
present consequence. It gives readers the source record and enough context to
judge the change.

The section is built for accountability. Humor may sharpen the telling once
the record is complete and fair.

## Reader expectation

Readers should see the evidence for themselves. A Receipts story must provide the original statement or the strongest available record, its date, its context, the later action, and the consequence of the gap between them.

The reader should finish knowing:

- who made the original claim;
- what the words meant at the time;
- what later changed or failed to happen;
- whether the person or institution offered an explanation;
- why the record matters now.

## What belongs

- Public promises that were broken or quietly abandoned.
- Roadmaps that materially missed their commitments.
- Political reversals with real policy consequences.
- Corporate conduct that conflicts with stated principles or representations.
- Influencer and public-figure contradictions that affect an audience, a business, or a public issue.
- Older statements that become relevant because of a current decision.

There is no expiration date. Age can add context, though every story still needs present relevance.

## What does not

- A harmless change of mind.
- A prediction made in good faith that proved wrong.
- A private person's old post revived for ridicule.
- Jokes, fragments, or screenshots stripped of their original context.
- A minor wording inconsistency with no consequence.
- A claim that was clearly corrected and fully addressed at the time, unless the correction itself is relevant.
- Personal hypocrisy that has no bearing on public conduct or the person's stated authority.
- A collection of embarrassing clips assembled mainly to provoke harassment.

## Typical length

Most stories run from 700 to 1,400 words. A single, well-documented contradiction may need 500 to 800. A pattern spanning years may require a longer chronology or a linked evidence file.

Use the shortest form that can establish the record, include the response, and explain the stakes.

## Tone

Use exact dates, quotes, and actions. Let the sequence carry more force than
outrage. Pointed writing is welcome when the evidence supports it.

Avoid gloating, mind-reading, and courtroom language that the reporting cannot
support. A correction should carry the same clarity as the original charge.

## Publishing philosophy

Build and verify the timeline before drawing a conclusion. Preserve the full
original source when lawful and practical. A reversal qualifies when the later
conduct conflicts materially with a public claim and the conflict matters now.
Changed circumstances and an on-record explanation belong in that test.

Seek a response before making a serious allegation, and include the strongest
relevant defense. A missed target supports a claim of failure. Calling it a lie
requires evidence of intent.

Old material is fair game when it illuminates a live issue. Its age never excuses weak relevance or missing context.

## Success metric

The durable record is the measure. A successful Receipts story should remain accurate when the immediate joke has faded and should help future reporting establish what happened.

Editors should audit:

- direct, dated support for each quoted promise or position;
- a complete enough timeline to avoid a false contradiction;
- fair inclusion of corrections, changed circumstances, and responses;
- a clear account of the public consequence;
- the severity and recurrence of errors, plus the speed and candor of
  corrections;
- whether later reporters and readers can use the evidence file without reconstructing it from scratch.

High engagement can accompany accountability. It cannot substitute for a sound record.

## Internal examples

- A company sells a product using a dated roadmap, misses the date, and removes
  the roadmap. Preserve each version and ask the company to account for the
  change.
- A politician campaigns against a power and later uses it in office. Compare
  the exact positions and determine whether the law or circumstances changed.
- A platform's enforcement guide permits conduct that its public moderation
  pledge condemns. Put both documents in front of the reader and report the
  effect on users.
- A public expert dismisses a practice, then sells a product built around it.
  The commercial consequence makes the change worth examining.

## Anti-examples

- An old joke treated as a policy commitment.
- Two quotations with similar words and different contexts presented as a reversal.
- A prediction that missed by a month framed as deliberate deceit.
- A private individual's embarrassing post republished because it is funny.
- A screenshot without a source, date, or archive.
- A headline that declares hypocrisy while the article never establishes a consequence.
- A subject contacted after publication so the story can claim they declined to comment.
